chapter.title: Managing Real-Time Public Transport Data (STIB)
chapter.para: The chapter on GTFS data builds the trips that the Brussels public transport company STIB-MIVB plans to run. This chapter loads the trips its vehicles actually ran: the positions of every bus, tram and metro, recorded every 20 seconds. It builds one trajectory per vehicle, explores a day of service, detects vehicles that stopped or crawled between stops, follows the vehicles live, and serves their trajectories as vector tiles for a map.

The data comes from MobilityTwin.Brussels, a platform of the CoDE laboratory of the Université libre de Bruxelles that collects the open mobility data of Brussels. It polls the real-time API of STIB-MIVB every 20 seconds, follows each vehicle from poll to poll, and matches it to the GTFS trip it is running. The platform keeps the history of these positions since April 2024, one Parquet file per day, together with the GTFS timetable that was valid on each day. Its documentation asks the users of the data to cite the paper MobilityTwin.Brussels by Gaspard Merten and Mahmoud Sakr (SIGSPATIAL 2023).

section.title: Contents
section.para:
This module covers the following topics:
Downloading a day of vehicle positions and its GTFS timetable
Building one trajectory per vehicle, with gaps, together with temporal attributes: the GTFS trip, the delay, and the status at a stop
Computing commercial speeds and delays per line
Detecting vehicles that stopped or crawled between stops
Appending the positions of the live feed to the trajectories
Serving the trajectories as Mapbox vector tiles

section.title: Getting the Data
section.para:
Using the API requires a token. Registration on MobilityTwin.Brussels is free, and the token is shown on the account page. The data is not bundled with the workshop: each reader downloads it with their own token. We use the positions of Monday 16 November 2026. The API returns the addresses of the Parquet files covering a time range, which are downloaded without a token. A file covers a day in UTC, that is, from 1:00 to 1:00 in Brussels.
export MOBILITYTWIN_TOKEN=<your token> API=https://api.mobilitytwin.brussels # The Parquet file of the vehicle positions of Monday 16 November 2026 (UTC) curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $MOBILITYTWIN_TOKEN" \ "$API/stib/vehicle-trip/parquet?start_timestamp=2026-11-16T00:00:00Z&end_timestamp=2026-11-17T00:00:00Z" # {"results": ["https://.../2026-11-16_00-00-00_to_2026-11-17_00-00-00.parquet"]} curl -s -o stib_2026-11-16.parquet \ https://motionlake.blob.core.windows.net/mobilitytwin/stib_vehicle_trip/2026-11-16_00-00-00_to_2026-11-17_00-00-00.parquet # The GTFS timetable that was valid on that day curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $MOBILITYTWIN_TOKEN" -o gtfs.zip \ "$API/stib/gtfs?timestamp=2026-11-16T12:00:00Z" unzip -q gtfs.zip -d gtfs

The Parquet file has one row per vehicle and per poll. Its main columns are the following:
uuid identifies a vehicle for as long as it is tracked on one run.
lineId and routeId are the line number and its GTFS route.
tripId is the GTFS trip the vehicle is running. It is empty until the vehicle has called at its second stop, since which waiting vehicle makes the next departure cannot be known from the feed. It is inferred by the platform as the best match to the timetable.
delay is the delay in seconds at the last stop called at, negative when early.
status is STOPPED_AT or IN_TRANSIT_TO, and empty on the metro.
timestamp is the time of the poll in Unix seconds, and lon and lat the position in WGS84.

We convert the Parquet file into a CSV file with DuckDB.
pip install duckdb python3 -c " import duckdb duckdb.sql('''COPY (SELECT uuid, lineId, directionId, direction, pointId, distanceFromPoint, routeId, timestamp, tripId, startDate, startTime, delay, status, stopId, stopSequence, lon, lat FROM 'stib_2026-11-16.parquet') TO 'stib_positions.csv' (HEADER)''')"

section.title: Loading the Positions
section.para:
We create a database stib with the extension, and set its time zone to the one of Brussels, in which all the times of this chapter are shown.
CREATE EXTENSION mobilitydb CASCADE; ALTER DATABASE stib SET TimeZone = 'Europe/Brussels'; We then connect again and load the CSV file, from the directory of the downloaded files.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS stib_input; CREATE TABLE stib_input ( uuid text, line_id text, direction_id text, direction integer, point_id text, distance_from_point float, route_id text, epoch double precision, trip_id text, start_date text, start_time text, delay integer, status text, stop_id text, stop_sequence integer, lon float, lat float ); \copy stib_input FROM 'stib_positions.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true)
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS stib_positions; CREATE TABLE stib_positions AS SELECT uuid AS vehicle_id, line_id, route_id, direction, trip_id, delay, status, to_timestamp(epoch) AS t, ST_Transform(ST_Point(lon, lat, 4326), 31370) AS geom FROM stib_input; CREATE INDEX ON stib_positions (vehicle_id, t); The table stib_positions keeps the columns we use, with the time as a timestamptz and the position in the Belgian Lambert 72 projection (EPSG:31370), so that distances are measured in metres.
SELECT count(*) AS positions, count(DISTINCT vehicle_id) AS runs, min(t), max(t) FROM stib_positions; -- positions | runs | min | max -- -----------+-------+-------------------------------+------------------------------ -- 2256768 | 24711 | 2026-11-16 01:00:00.109004+01 | 2026-11-17 00:59:59.22366+01 -- (1 row)

section.title: Building the Trajectories
section.para:
We build one row per vehicle run, with its trajectory and three temporal attributes.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS stib_vehicles; CREATE TABLE stib_vehicles AS SELECT vehicle_id, line_id, route_id, appendInstant(tgeompoint(geom, t), 'linear', 1000.0, interval '2 minutes' ORDER BY t) AS trip, appendInstant(ttext(trip_id, t), 'step', interval '2 minutes' ORDER BY t) FILTER (WHERE trip_id IS NOT NULL) AS trip_id, appendInstant(tint(delay, t), 'step', NULL, interval '2 minutes' ORDER BY t) FILTER (WHERE delay IS NOT NULL) AS delay, appendInstant(ttext(status, t), 'step', interval '2 minutes' ORDER BY t) FILTER (WHERE status IS NOT NULL) AS status FROM stib_positions GROUP BY vehicle_id, line_id, route_id;
DELETE FROM stib_vehicles WHERE numInstants(trip) = 1; UPDATE stib_vehicles v SET trip = (SELECT tgeompointSeqSet(array_agg(s ORDER BY startTimestamp(s))) FROM unnest(sequences(v.trip)) AS s WHERE numInstants(s) > 1) WHERE numSequences(v.trip) > 1; DELETE FROM stib_vehicles WHERE trip IS NULL; CREATE INDEX ON stib_vehicles USING gist (trip); The aggregate function appendInstant appends the positions of a run in time order. Its arguments give the interpolation, linear for the position and step for the attributes, and the gaps: a new sequence starts when two consecutive positions are more than 1,000 metres or 2 minutes apart, so that the trajectory does not invent a path across a missing stretch of data. A temporal text trip_id keeps the GTFS trip of the run over time, since a run can carry several trips and a trip can be carried by several runs when the platform loses a vehicle and finds it again. A temporal integer delay and a temporal text status keep the delay and the status at a stop. The trajectory keeps only the positions it needs: a position on the straight line between its neighbours at the matching time adds nothing.
SELECT count(*) AS runs, sum(numInstants(trip)) AS instants, sum(numSequences(trip)) AS sequences, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('stib_vehicles')) AS size FROM stib_vehicles; -- runs | instants | sequences | size -- -------+----------+-----------+------- -- 23875 | 1513338 | 26844 | 79 MB -- (1 row) The day's 2,256,768 positions become 1,513,338 instants. A run made of a single position, and an isolated position between two gaps, describe no movement and are removed by the DELETE and UPDATE statements above.

section.title: Loading the Routes and Stops
section.para:
From the GTFS timetable of the day we only need the routes, which give the mode of each line, and the stops.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS routes; CREATE TABLE routes ( route_id text PRIMARY KEY, agency_id text, route_short_name text, route_long_name text, route_desc text, route_type integer, route_url text, route_color text, route_text_color text ); \copy routes FROM 'gtfs/routes.txt' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true)
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS stops; CREATE TABLE stops ( stop_id text PRIMARY KEY, stop_code text, stop_name text, stop_desc text, stop_lat float, stop_lon float, zone_id text, stop_url text, location_type integer, parent_station text, wheelchair_boarding integer ); \copy stops FROM 'gtfs/stops.txt' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true) ALTER TABLE stops ADD COLUMN stop_geom geometry(Point, 31370); UPDATE stops SET stop_geom = ST_Transform(ST_Point(stop_lon, stop_lat, 4326), 31370); CREATE INDEX ON stops USING gist (stop_geom); The column route_type is 0 for the tram, 1 for the metro and 3 for the bus. The chapter on GTFS data shows how to build the planned trips from the rest of the timetable, to compare them with the trips that ran.

section.title: Exploring a Day of Service
section.para:
The commercial speed of each mode is the distance its vehicles travelled divided by the time they were tracked, stops and layovers included.
SELECT CASE r.route_type WHEN 0 THEN 'tram' WHEN 1 THEN 'metro' ELSE 'bus' END AS mode, count(*) AS runs, round(sum(length(trip)) / 1000) AS km, round((sum(length(trip)) / extract(epoch FROM sum(duration(trip))) * 3.6)::numeric, 1) AS kmh FROM stib_vehicles v JOIN routes r USING (route_id) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1; -- mode | runs | km | kmh -- -------+-------+-------+------ -- bus | 15151 | 82947 | 10.0 -- metro | 1453 | 14424 | 18.7 -- tram | 7271 | 45021 | 11.1 -- (3 rows) The metro is only observed at its stations, so its trajectory is the straight line between consecutive stations, which slightly underestimates its distance.

The slowest lines during the morning peak are obtained by restricting the trajectories to the period from 8:00 to 9:00 with the function atTime. The operator && keeps the runs whose bounding box overlaps the period, using the GiST index of the table.
SELECT line_id, count(*) AS runs, round((sum(length(atTime(trip, p))) / extract(epoch FROM sum(duration(atTime(trip, p)))) * 3.6)::numeric, 1) AS kmh FROM stib_vehicles, LATERAL (SELECT tstzspan '[2026-11-16 08:00, 2026-11-16 09:00)' AS p) AS s WHERE trip && p GROUP BY line_id HAVING count(*) >= 10 ORDER BY kmh LIMIT 5; -- line_id | runs | kmh -- ---------+------+----- -- T81 | 23 | 7.1 -- 34 | 31 | 7.5 -- 64 | 24 | 7.9 -- 86 | 32 | 8.0 -- 29 | 32 | 8.2 -- (5 rows)

The trajectory of one GTFS trip is the part of a run during which its temporal attribute trip_id had the trip as value. The operator ?= keeps the runs that ever carried the trip, and the function whenTrue returns the periods during which the trip was carried.
SELECT vehicle_id, startTimestamp(whenTrue(trip_id #= '134460577341186002'::text))::time(0) AS since, round(length(atTime(trip, whenTrue(trip_id #= '134460577341186002'::text)))) AS metres, duration(whenTrue(trip_id #= '134460577341186002'::text))::interval(0) AS duration FROM stib_vehicles WHERE trip_id ?= '134460577341186002'::text ORDER BY since; -- vehicle_id | since | metres | duration -- --------------------------------------+----------+--------+---------- -- 022ff490-1234-4635-bf73-48f8003afa7a | 08:04:02 | 1845 | 00:10:28 -- b58377f3-6e03-4d18-ae0a-e1735a79ee9d | 08:14:30 | 5642 | 00:29:26 -- (2 rows) The trip was carried by two runs: the platform lost the vehicle after 1.8 kilometres and found it again as a new run.

The time-weighted average of the delay, computed with the function twAvg, weighs each value by how long it held, and the function maxValue returns the largest delay of a run.
SELECT line_id, round((avg(twAvg(delay)) / 60)::numeric, 1) AS avg_delay_min, max(maxValue(delay)) / 60 AS max_delay_min FROM stib_vehicles WHERE delay IS NOT NULL GROUP BY line_id ORDER BY avg_delay_min DESC LIMIT 5; -- line_id | avg_delay_min | max_delay_min -- ---------+---------------+--------------- -- 36 | 2.2 | 17 -- 77 | 2.1 | 12 -- 75 | 1.9 | 22 -- 73 | 1.9 | 12 -- 79 | 1.9 | 22 -- (5 rows)

section.title: Detecting Incidents
section.para:
A vehicle that stays still for several minutes away from any stop is a sign of an incident: a breakdown, an accident, or a blocked track. The function stops returns the parts of a trajectory during which the vehicle stayed within a given distance, here 20 metres, for at least a given duration, here 3 minutes. We ignore the metro, which is only observed at its stations, the stops at the start and at the end of a run, which are layovers at a terminus, and the stops within 50 metres of a stop of the network. The status of the feed cannot replace this last test: a vehicle waiting at a terminus can be reported IN_TRANSIT_TO its first stop.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS stopped; CREATE TABLE stopped AS SELECT v.vehicle_id, v.line_id, s.stop FROM stib_vehicles v JOIN routes r USING (route_id), unnest(sequences(stops(v.trip, 20.0, interval '3 minutes'))) AS s(stop) WHERE r.route_type <> 1 AND startTimestamp(s.stop) > startTimestamp(v.trip) AND endTimestamp(s.stop) < endTimestamp(v.trip) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM stops p WHERE ST_DWithin(p.stop_geom, startValue(s.stop), 50.0)); SELECT count(*) AS alarms, count(DISTINCT vehicle_id) AS vehicles FROM stopped; SELECT line_id, startTimestamp(stop)::time(0) AS since, duration(stop)::interval(0) AS stopped_for, n.stop_name AS nearest_stop, round(ST_Distance(startValue(stop), n.stop_geom)) AS metres FROM stopped, LATERAL (SELECT stop_name, stop_geom FROM stops ORDER BY stop_geom <-> startValue(stop) LIMIT 1) AS n ORDER BY duration(stop) DESC LIMIT 5; -- alarms | vehicles -- --------+---------- -- 755 | 705 -- (1 row) -- -- line_id | since | stopped_for | nearest_stop | metres -- ---------+----------+-------------+-----------------+-------- -- 42 | 14:19:53 | 00:39:09 | VIADUC E40 | 54 -- 89 | 15:33:49 | 00:29:04 | DELACROIX | 205 -- 87 | 19:31:36 | 00:28:39 | GARE DE BERCHEM | 108 -- 95 | 09:18:17 | 00:26:46 | SCIENCE | 88 -- T81 | 16:14:15 | 00:24:59 | CONSEIL | 60 -- (5 rows)

A vehicle crawling in traffic moves, but slowly. The function speed returns the speed of a trajectory in metres per second as a temporal float, the comparison #< returns a temporal Boolean that is true while the speed is below 5 km/h, and the function whenTrue returns the periods during which it is true. We keep the periods of at least 5 minutes during which the vehicle moved at least 50 metres, which leaves out the time spent at a stop.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS slowed; CREATE TABLE slowed AS SELECT v.vehicle_id, v.line_id, p AS period, length(atTime(v.trip, p)) AS metres FROM stib_vehicles v JOIN routes r USING (route_id), unnest(spans(whenTrue(speed(v.trip) #< 5 / 3.6))) AS p WHERE r.route_type <> 1 AND duration(p) >= interval '5 minutes' AND length(atTime(v.trip, p)) >= 50.0; SELECT extract(hour FROM lower(period)) AS hour, count(*) AS alarms FROM slowed GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1; -- hour | alarms -- ------+-------- -- 0 | 2 -- 5 | 1 -- 6 | 4 -- 7 | 18 -- 8 | 30 -- 9 | 45 -- 10 | 4 -- 11 | 17 -- 12 | 12 -- 13 | 10 -- 14 | 11 -- 15 | 20 -- 16 | 46 -- 17 | 67 -- 18 | 45 -- 19 | 8 -- 20 | 7 -- 21 | 4 -- 22 | 3 -- 23 | 1 -- (20 rows) The alarms concentrate in the morning and in the evening peaks.

section.title: Following the Vehicles Live
Serving Vector Tiles
section.para:
A map shows the trajectories as Mapbox vector tiles. The following function returns the tile z/x/y of the trajectories during a period. The function asMVTGeom clips a trajectory to the tile and returns its geometry in tile coordinates together with the time of each of its points, which a client uses to animate the vehicles.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION stib_tile(z integer, x integer, y integer, p_start timestamptz, p_end timestamptz) RETURNS bytea AS $$ WITH bounds AS ( SELECT ST_TileEnvelope(z, x, y) AS geom ), vals AS ( SELECT v.vehicle_id, v.line_id, asMVTGeom(transform(s, 3857), stbox(b.geom)) AS geom_times FROM stib_vehicles v, bounds b, unnest(sequences(atTime(v.trip, span(p_start, p_end)))) AS s WHERE v.trip && stbox(ST_Transform(b.geom, 31370), span(p_start, p_end)) ), mvtgeom AS ( SELECT (geom_times).geom, (geom_times).times, vehicle_id, line_id FROM vals WHERE GeometryType((geom_times).geom) <> 'GEOMETRYCOLLECTION' ) SELECT ST_AsMVT(mvtgeom) FROM mvtgeom; $$ LANGUAGE sql STABLE PARALLEL SAFE; Each sequence of a trajectory is a feature of its own. When the part of a sequence inside the tile is made of lines and of an isolated position, asMVTGeom returns a collection of lines and a point, which a vector tile cannot encode; the function leaves these rare pieces out.
SELECT length(stib_tile(13, 4195, 2748, '2026-11-16 08:00', '2026-11-16 08:15')) AS bytes; -- bytes -- ------- -- 61423 -- (1 row) A tile server that publishes PostgreSQL functions, such as pg_tileserv or Martin, serves this function to a web map.
